faq.q: When should I switch from IV fluids to oral/enteral feeding?

faq.a: Balanced crystalloid (Ringer's lactate) to avoid worsening acidosis; give blood transfusion if Hb < 7 g/dL.
faq.q: What fluid is best for a patient with severe malaria and anaemia?

faq.a: It can cause hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis and renal vasoconstriction.

exam: A patient with HIV‑related cachexia needs nutrition – why is enteral feeding preferred over parenteral? — Preserves gut mucosal immunity, lower infection risk, cheaper, and provides trophic hormones.
What electrolyte abnormality is most likely after massive blood transfusion and how do you prevent it? — Hypocalcaemia from citrate; give calcium gluconate if ionised Ca < 1.0 mmol/L.

A postoperative patient develops abdominal distension and high nasogastric output – what does this indicate and how do you manage it? — Possible ileus or anastomotic leak; stop oral intake, keep NG tube, give IV fluids, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and arrange imaging.

When is parenteral nutrition absolutely indicated in a surgical patient? — When the gut cannot be used for >7 days (e.g., high‑grade bowel obstruction, severe pancreatitis) and the patient is malnourished.

Explain why balanced crystalloids reduce the risk of acute kidney injury compared with normal saline. — Lower chloride load avoids renal vasoconstriction and hyperchloraemic acidosis, preserving renal perfusion.
ai.title: Surgical Nutrition and Fluid Therapy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Effective nutrition and fluid management are essential for surgical patients, especially in low‑resource settings where malnutrition and dehydration are common. Understanding assessment, choice of fluids, and nutrition routes helps prevent complications and supports recovery.

b: Goal: maintain euvolemia, correct electrolyte deficits, and provide adequate calories/protein.
Common local issues: malaria‑related anemia, HIV‑associated malnutrition, TB, chronic diarrhoea, herbal medicine use.
sections.p: Surgical patients often lose fluids and nutrients through fasting, blood loss, vomiting, or sepsis. In low‑resource hospitals, limited lab tests and intravenous (IV) solutions make clinical judgment crucial.

b: Fluid types: isotonic crystalloids (0.9% saline, Ringer's lactate) vs. hypotonic solutions (5% dextrose) for maintenance.
Nutrition routes: oral > enteral (NG/OG tube) > parenteral (TPN) when gut cannot be used.
sections.p: Assess volume status, nutritional risk, and ongoing losses. Choose crystalloids for resuscitation, colloids only when hypo‑albuminaemia is severe, and start enteral nutrition within 24 h if gut is functional.

b: Identify high‑risk patients: BMI < 18.5, recent weight loss >10 %, serum albumin < 30 g/L.
Prioritise early enteral feeding to preserve gut integrity and reduce infection risk.
sections.p: Inadequate fluid therapy leads to hypovolaemic shock, acute kidney injury, or pulmonary oedema. Poor nutrition increases wound infection, anastomotic leak, and mortality.

t.b: Is the patient hypovolaemic? – Delayed >2 seconds suggests poor perfusion; treat with bolus crystalloids.
Detect hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, or metabolic acidosis – guide fluid composition; if unavailable, use clinical clues (muscle cramps, arrhythmia).
Is renal perfusion adequate? – <0.5 mL/kg/h indicates under‑resuscitation; give additional fluid.

b: Use the 4‑2‑1 rule for maintenance fluids: 4 mL/kg for first 10 kg, 2 mL/kg for next 10 kg, 1 mL/kg thereafter.
For a 55‑kg patient: 4 × 10 + 2 × 10 + 1 × 35 = 95 mL/h of isotonic fluid.
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to choose fluids, calculate maintenance needs, and recognise when to switch to enteral or parenteral nutrition.

t.b: Is protein deficiency severe? – <30 g/L suggests need for protein‑rich enteral feeds or albumin infusion if hypo‑albuminaemic shock.
Is hyperglycaemia present? – >180 mg/dL warrants insulin infusion; low glucose (<70 mg/dL) needs dextrose.

b: Giving large volumes of 0.9% saline → hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis; prefer balanced crystalloids.
Starting parenteral nutrition before a functional gut – increases infection risk.
Neglecting electrolyte replacement when using large dextrose solutions.
sections.p: Errors often arise from over‑resuscitation, inappropriate fluid choice, or delayed nutrition.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe sepsis with hypotension despite 2 L fluid bolus
Acute respiratory distress from fluid overload
